ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
FDI in assets reconstruction companies 
*41. SHRI C. RAMAGHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to allow Foreign Direct 
Investment (FDI) upto 49 per cent in Assets Reconstruction Companies (ARCs) 
set up to buy non-performing assets from banks; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; 
(c) the number of cases handed over to the above company for disposal 
by banks and financial institutions; 
(d) the amount of funds involved in these cases; 
(e) the funds to be received by Banks/FIs; and 
(f) the time limit set for disposal of cases? 

RAJYA SABHA [21 February, 2006] 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (f) 
A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The Government of India, vide press release dated 
November 8,2005 has permitted Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) upto 49 per 
cent in the equity capital of Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs) 
registered with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). The permission has been 
accorded with a view to facilitate resolution of Non-Performing Assets 
(NPAs) of the Indian banking system by the ARCs and to enhance the 
possibility of banks realising better value for their NPAs drawing from the 
expertise and resources of foreign institutions having international experience 
in management of stressed assets. 
(c) and (d) None of the four ARCs granted Certificate of Registration 
by the RBI so far has any FDI participation in its equity. Asset 
Reconstruction Company (India) Limited (ARCIL) is the only ARC that has 
commenced its operations. ARCIL ha s reported that as on December 
31,2005, they had acquired 375 cases from banks/FIs having total due of Rs. 
17,783/- crore from 27 banks/FIs at an acquisition price of Rs. 4,359/- crore. 
(e)The amount realized by the Bank no rmally is the price received by 
it from the ARC acquiring the stressed assets plus a percentage of the net 
gain realized on the disposal of the reconstructed assets by the ARC. 
(f) RBI has specified a five year timefra me for realization of assets by 
ARCs from the date of acquisition. 
SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Sir, it is a very good concept that has 
been introduced in our country by creating ARCs for realising the bad debts 
of the banks. Sir, in this process we ha ve issued security receipts to the banks 
from whom the bad debts are being purchased. So, my first supplementary is 
this. The very purpose of issuing the security receipt* is to enhance the 
realisable value of the NPAs. If such is the case whether there is any thinking 
on the part of the Government to allow th ese security receipts to be traded in 
the stock market so that the Flls enter the market and trade all these 
securities, so that the liquidity of both the ARCs and the banks can be 
improved which is the purpose of creating these ARCs. 
2 

[21 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, the Securities Act is being amended and 
the amendment is now pending. It is part of the Bill that securitised debts must 
be traded on the capital market. Once the Bill is passed by Parliament, that 
will happen. 
SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Sir, my  second aspect of the first 
supplementary has not been answered, th at is, whether Flls will be allowed 
to operate in the stock market.  
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: That is  only after the amendment is 
passed. We cannot anticipate an amendment to be passed by Parliament. Once the 
amendment is passed, then we will lay down the guidelines. 
SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Sir, my second supplementary is this. 
Thanks to the Finance Minister and his predecessors who have reduced these 
NPAs from 6.5 per cent in 2001 to 1 per cent in 2005-06, as per the data that is 
available. But how much is by way of recovery? You were able to reduce 5 per 
cent of the total advances as NPAs—how much is by way of recovery, how 
much assets the banks have sold to these ARCs and how much amount has 
been written off. You see the very purpose is to clinch the balance sheet. So, 
how much of it has been written off, how much has been collected and how 
much has been sold to the ARCs? 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Although it strictly does not arise out of this 
question, but let me attempt an answer. What is being sold to the ARC, that is 
actually only one ARC, which has effectively started functioning now, namely, 
ARCIL. I have given the particulars in paragraphs (c) and (d) of the answer. But 
that represents only a small portion of the NPAs. ARCs will take root and will 
expand their operations hopefully in this calendar year or the next financial 
year. As far as reduction of the NPAs is concerned, the hon. Member is 
absolutely right. The reduction happens in three ways. 
One is by recovery. One is by write off. In write off, there are two kinds 
of write off. One is a t echnical right off where the loan is still shown on the 
books of the bank at a nominal value of rupee one and the other is a complete 
write off and the third is by up-gradation. Now I am not in a position to give 
you now although I have the figures, bank-wise figures. Broadly speaking, I 
have insisted with public sector banks that the amount actually written off should 
not be larger than the amount of cash recovery in that year. Most banks are able 
to make cash recovery and we are

think these are matters which should be left to the market. We cannot decide 
the price of NPA unless we look at the quality and appetite in the market.

[21 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, the total amount of non-performing 
assets of public sector banks as at the end of March 2005 is Rs. 47,696 crores of 
which the Nationalised Banks is Rs. 31,964 crores and State Bank group is Rs. 
14,804 crores and IDBI is Rs. 924 crores. These figures can be furnished even 
bank-wise if the hon. Member wants. So, I think there is a misunderstanding or 
maybe 1 did not communicate effectively. There are two separate issues. What is 
being sold now by NPAs to ARCs is about Rs. 17,000 worth of NPAs, actually 
Rs. 17,783 crores of NPA has been Sold to the ARC for Rs. 4359 crores. 
That is a separate transaction. The difference, of course, as Mr. Ramachandraiah 
says has to be written off. Each Dank Will write it off from the balance sheet. 
Each bank Will write It off from its balance sheet. But, the bulk of this 
is really from the private sector banks. So , really, it is for the private sector 
banks to decide what is right or wrong. 
The other part of the answer which I gave was, as a general guideline. I 
have told public sector banks that when you write off an amount, finally and 
fully, make sure that in the same year the recovery department is able Jo recover 
from other NPAs, at least, an amount equal to the amount you are writing Off. If 
a bank proposed to write off, say about Rs. 500 crores of NPA fully I want 
the bank to ensure that the recovery department recovers, at least, Rs. 500 
crores in that year from other NPAs so that the recovery and the write off are 
more or less equal so that owner's funds are not affected. These are two 
separate issues.

Bilateral agreement with China in oil sector 
*43. SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI:†  
SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: 
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether India has entered into a bilateral agreement with China aiming 
at co-operation between the two nations on exploration and production of oil, 
downstream products, strategic storage and stockpiling, research and 
development, conservation and promotion of environment-friendly fuels; and 
(b) if so, what distinct advantage India would be getting through this 
agreement annually beginning from year 2006 towards fulfilling the ever-
increasing demand for petroleum products, etc. in quantitative terms and 
provision of qualitative environment-friendly fuels like coal-bed methane, coal-
gasification and hydrates, etc.? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI 
MURLI DEORA): (a) to (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. A Memorandum for Cooperation in the field of Oil 
and Natural Gas between the National Development & Reforms Commission 
of the Peoples' Republic of China and the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural 
Gas of the Republic of India was signed on 12th January, 2006. In addition, 
GAIL (India) Ltd., have signed three MoUs with SINOPEC, CNOOC 
(International) Limited and Beijing Gas Company Ltd., respectively, while the 
Directorate General of Hydrocarbons has signed an MoU with the Research 
Institute of Petroleum Exploration and Development (RIPED)  of China to 
enhance cooperation on oil and gas related issues of mutual interest and to 
exchange information in the development of policy on oil and gas exploration 
and production. Again, OVL have signed an agreement with CNODC Ltd., the 
international arm 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shrimati Mohsina 
Kidwai. 
6 

[21 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
of the National Oil Company, CNPC Ltd., for co-operation in the field of E&P 
activities in third countries. 
The areas of cooperation envisaged in the Memorandum of Cooperation 
entered into between the two Governments are as follows: 
(i) promote cooperation between the companies and organisations of both 
countries in oil and natural gas production, execution of large 
engineering projects, and manufacturing, upgradation and supply of 
drilling equipment and petrochemical processing units; 
(ii) encourage bilateral cooperation for undertaking joint exploration and 
production initiatives for oil and natural gas resources in 
third countries; 
(iii) encourage cooperation on basic and applied R&D; 
(iv) encourage bilateral cooperative relationship in the areas of crude oil 
trade and transportation and to study the development of the Asian 
crude oil and oil products markets, and the measures required to 
stabilize the Asian oil markets with the aim of enhancing the 
influence of both nations in the world crude oil pricing mechanism 
and promoting a stable supply and demand mechanism in the Asian 
energy market; 
(v) encourage exchange of informat ion and experience on commercial 
stockpiling of oil between the companies and organizations of both 
countries; 
(vi) encourage collaboration between the companies and organisations of 
both countries in heavy oil; 
(vii) encourage cooperation in areas such as coal bed methane, 
underground coal gasification and gas hydrates; and 
(viii) exchange of information on policies and programmes on the 
sustainable development of oil and natural gas industries. 
The memorandum provides for the setting of a Joint Working Group at 
official level to identify and pursue these areas of cooperation. 
On the basis of the bilateral Government-to-Government MoU and the 
company-to-company MoUs which have been finalised or are presently under 
consideration, India and China, as principal consumers of hydrocarbon 
resources in Asia, have committed themselves to a long- 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [21 February, 2006] 
term and substantial partnership to enhance each others' capabilities and 
resources and to jointly pursue their interests at the international, regional and 
bilateral fora. In this endeavour, the two countries are bringing together their 
technical, financial and human resources in order to obtain their common 
interests of serve their national energy security interests. 
The specific areas in which this cooperation will manifest itself in the 
coming years are: 
(i) participation in upstream and do wnstream projects in each others' 
countries; 
(ii) pursue investment opprtunities in third countries by submitting joint 
bids for equity participation in oil producing fields or seeking E&P 
contracts; 
(iii) enhancing domestic capabilities a nd resources through joint pursuit 
of R&D proposals particularly in th e areas of increased oil recovery 
and enhanced oil recovery in order to boost domestic production; 
(iv) mobilise national capacities in the areas of Engineering and 
Petroleum services through join t ventures both in each others' 
countries and in third countries; 
(v) bring together their significant position in the international oil 
market by exploring the possibility of joint purchases of crude oil 
and gas; 
(vi) pursue studies jointly to bring about important changes in the 
organisation and functioning of the Asian Oil Markets in order to make 
them more transparent and more reflective of the realities of the 
contemporary oil scenario in which Asian consuming countries are 
the consumers of the bulk of Asian oil production and yet have to 
function in a market environmen t that is non-transparent and 
iniquitous; 
(vii) pursue research and technology  development projects in the area of 
unconventional energy resources such as the development of Coal 
Bed Methane (CBM) and Gas Hydrates; 
(viii) participate in transnational oil and gas pipelines projects to transport 
hydrocarbon resources from Asian producing centres to the principal 
Asian consuming countries; and 
8 

[21 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(ix) pursue joint projects in the areas of conservation and development 
Of environment friendly fuels. 
The proposed cooperation between India and China in the hydrocarbon 
sector is wide ranging and promises to yield enormous, benefits to the two countries 
on account of their pulling together their formidable resources and acting jointly in 
pursuit of their common interests.

Statement 
(a) and (b) Exploration for crude oil and natural gas in the Himalayan region 
started as early as 1956 especially in the State of Himachal Pradesh soon after the 
inception of Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited (ONGC). The entire 
Himalayan foothills have remained under active exploration because of 
known surface oil shows at Choumukha near S undemagar and historical gas 
show near Jwalaji temple, Jwalamukhi. 
Since inception, ONGC has acquired 8,198 Ground Line Kilometres (GLK) 
of 2D seismic data and frilled 19 wells in the Himalayan foothills region 
falling in the State of Himachal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir, Punjab and Uttar 
Pradesh. However, there has not been any commercial success so far. During 
Tenth Plan period, ONGC envisaged to acquire 225 GLK 2D seismic data and 
drill three exploratory wells in the region. ONGC has already acquired 605 GLK 
Of 2D seismic data and drilled two exploratory wells in Himachal Pradesh. Oil 
lndia Limited (OIL) has also acquired about 2,786 GLK of 2D seismic data in 
Himalayan Foothills in Uttaranchal. To supplement the exploration efforts, 
Directorate General Qf Hydrocarbons (DGH) has also acquired 24,000 
Kilometres of aeromagnetic survey data  falling in the State of Himachal 
Pradesh and Punjab. 
During second phase of explorat ion in the block HF-ONN-200/1 in 
Himachal Pradesh awarded under the third round of New Exploration 
Licensing Policy (NELP), ONGC plans to acquire 60 GLK of 2D seismic and 
drill one exploratory well. OIL plans to drill one exploratory well in 
Uttaranchal. 
The planned investment on exploration activities by ONGC in 
Himachal Pradesh and OIL in Uttaranc hal is about Rs. 45 crore and Rs. 35 
crore respectively. 
Hydrocarbon exploration is a high rise and high reward activity; in 
which while exploratory inputs remain determinable, results in terms of 
discoveries are highly probabilistic and therefore success of exploration efforts 
can not be predicted.

structure, it is possible to lend at about 7 or 7.5 per cent because at every level 
there is a cost of administration. Unfortunately, as the Vaidyanathan 
Committee Report brings out, the cooperative credit structure is virtually in a 
shambles. And, that is why, with the approval of the hon. Prime Minister, we 
have announced a Rs. 13,500 crores package for revamping the cooperative credit 
structure. Pending that revamping, which is being designed with the 
consultation of State Governments, we have now to ensure that banks lend—
banks borrow from NABARD at 5.5 to 5.75 per cent—at a reasonable rate. 
My distinguished colleague, Shri Janardhana Poojary, is absolutely right. The 
Karnataka State Government subsidises the interest rate and, therefore, they are 
able to lend at six per cent. Recently, the Government of Tamil Nadu has offered 
the subsidy, and I believe, they will also lend at six per cent. 
...(interruptions).... Some other State Governments are offering a subsidy. 
The point is, should the Central Government step in and fix the interest 
rate. My respectful submission is, that would not be a wise thing to do. The 
correct thing to do is to bring down inflation, bring down the cost of funds 
and, therefore, enable the banks to lend at a lower rate.

That is the wise and prudent course to follow, in order to maintain macro-
economic stability, and, at the same time, ensure that funds flow to the 
agricultural sector. 
It is true that car loans and refrig erator loans are available at a lower 
rate. Nobody denies that. But there is an important distinction. I am not trying to 
make a judgement here. There is an important distinction between this loan 
and that loan. A car loan is a collater alised loan. The car can be repossessed. 
Therefore, banks have a lower risk. They think they have a lower risk in 
lending to a person who wants to buy a car, or where there is a salary 
certificate. It is the risks involved in a sector, the cost of refinance and the cost 
of administration, which determine the interest rate.

administration.

VAT on biscuits 
207. SHRI B. K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether ketchup, cheese and butter are free from levy of excise duty; 
(b) if so, what is the rationale behind imposing VAT and excise on 
common man's nutrition food like biscuits costing less than Rs. 50.000 per 
kg;and 
(c) whether Government would consider freeing nutritional biscuits of 
low value from the levy VAT and excise in the larger interests of the people 
living below poverty line?. 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI S. S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) So far as VAT on biscuits is concerned, taxes on sale or purchase of 
goods is a State subject. An Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers 
has been constituted to take decisions on all matters relating to State level VAT 
and sales tax related issues. The rates of tax in a VAT regime, classification of 
goods for taxation etc. are subjects to be decided 
67 

RAJYA SABHA [21 February, 2006] 
upon by the Empowered Committee. The Empowered Committee has 
decided that the rate of VAT on biscuits shall be 12.5%. 
So far as rationale behind imposition of excise duty on biscuits is 
concerned, major raw material/inputs for manufacturing biscuits are wheat flour, 
vanaspati, preservatives and sugar, which are non perishable in nature,whereas 
raw materials used in ketchup, sauces, jams, juices, cheese and butter are 
perishable fruits, vegetables, milk and cream. Emphasis of the Government is 
for efficient and maximum utilization of perishable farm produce. 
(c) As stated in reply to part (b) above, the Empowered Committee has 
decided that the rate of VAT on biscuits shall be 12.5%. 
As regards excise duty, small scale/tiny units having annual turnover of less 
than Rs. 4 crore (during preceding financia l year) are eligible for excise duty 
exemption on clearance of Rs. one crore in a financial year. The request for 
exempting biscuits from excise duty was examined and it was felt that apart 
from revenue loss, general exemption from whole of excise duty would remove 
the advantage available to the unorganized sector. Since imported biscuits are 
charged to CVO, equal to that of excise duty, a general exemption from whole of 
excise duty would reduce the protection level to domestic industry, as in that 
case CVD on imported biscuits will become nil, whereas the domestic 
manufacturers will have to bear inputs taxes in the range of 4% to 6%.

Pojicy on disinvestment of Government companies 
209. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any concrete policy to disinvest 
Government companies; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government desire to disinvest profit-making companies and 
Navaratna companies earlier than loss-making companies; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI S. S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) and (b) The National Common 
Minimum Programme (NCMP) adopted by the Government outlines the policy 
of the Government with respect to the Public Sector, including disinvestment 
of Government's equity in Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs). The salient 
features of NCMP in this regard are as follows:— 
(i) The Government is committed to a strong and effective public 
sector whose social objectives are met by its commercial 
functioning. But for this, there is need for selectivity and a 
strategic focus, the Government is pledged to devolve full 
managerial and commercial autonomy to successful, profit-making 
companies operating in a competitive environment. Generally 
profit-making companies will not be privatised. 
(ii) All privatizations will be considered on a transparent and 
consultative case-by-case basis. The Government will retain 
69 

RAJYA SABHA [21 February, 2006] 
existing "navratna" companies in the public sector while these 
companies raise resources from the capital market. While every effort 
will be made to modernize and restructure sick public sector 
companies and revive sick industry, chronically loss-making 
companies will either be sold-off, or closed, after all workers have 
got their legitimate dues and compensation. The Government will 
induct private industry to turn around companies that have 
potential for revival. 
(iii) The Government believes that privatization should increase 
competition, not decrease it. It will not support the emergence of any 
monopoly that only restricts competition. It also believes that there 
must be a direct link between privatization and social needs like, for 
example, the use of privatization revenues for designated social 
sector schemes. Public sector companies and nationalized banks 
will be encouraged to enter the capital market to raise resources and 
offer new investment avenues to retail investors. 
(c) and (d) Disinvestment decisions are taken by the Government 
on a case by case basis in accordanc e with the policy mentioned above. 
While chronically loss-making companies will either be sold off or closed, 
small portions of equity in profit-making non-navratna public sector 
enterprises are proposed to be disinvested in order to raise resources 
for the National Investment Fund.

IPO scam 
232. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have unearthed IPO scam with 
fictitious demat accounts; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
95 

RAJYA SABHA [21 February, 2006] 
(c) the action taken against the offenders; and 
(d) the steps taken to ensure that there is no recurrence of such seam? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL): (a) a nd (b) Securities and Exchange 
Board of India (SEBI) has noticed certain irregularities in the issue of Initial 
Public Offering (IPO) shares in the recent past while examining the dealings in 
shares relating to the IPOs of the Yes Bank Ltd, and Infrastructure 
Development Finance Company Ltd. (IDFC). The enquiries and investigations 
made so far by Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and SEBI seem to indicate that a few 
entities opened thousands of demat accounts with Depository Participants (DPs) 
and bank accounts with Banks in the names of fictitious/benami individuals. 
They applied for shares in IPOs from these benami/fictitious accounts in sizes 
permissible for retail individual investors (Rlls) and obtained allotment. As a 
result, some genuine Rlls failed to get allotment or got allotment of fewer 
shares than they would have otherwise got. 
(c) and (d) The penal actions ta ken by SEBI include: debarring 
concerned entities from dealing in securities market/dealing in IPO; directing 
the concerned DPs not to open fresh demat accounts till further directions; 
directing the Depositories to enhance their surveillance system, and ordering 
inspection of the concerned Registrar to Issue and the Merchant Bankers. In 
order to prevent recurrence of the irregularities, the measures taken by SEBI 
include: directing the Depositories to advise their respective DPs to verify the 
genuineness of the demat account-holders where 20 or more demat accpunt-
holders have a common address; advising them to identify all the other IPOs 
during 2004 and 2005 wherein the same modus operandi could have been 
adopted by the identified entities; directing them to form a co-ordination 
committee to co-ordinate with the surveillance department of SEBI for 
monitoring abnormal transactions in demat accounts; and advising them that in 
case of IPOs they should activate the Indian Securities Numbering System 
only on the date of commencement of trading on the stock exchanges. 
The penal actions taken by RBI include imposition of penalties ranging 
from Rs. 5 lakh to Rs. 20 lakh against 7 Banks taking into account the extent and 
enormity of the violation of the RBI guidelines. Other measures include: 
advising all scheduled commercial banks, excluding 
96 

[21 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
RRBs, to conduct a review of IPO financing and related matters, like opening of 
multiple accouots, adherence to Know Your Client (KYC)/ Anti-Money Laundering 
(AML) guidelines and RBI instructions on IPO financing, advances against shares, 
etc.; prohibiting the Banks from crediting account payee cheques to account of any 
person other than the payee named therein; and taking up an examination of the 
internal control systems and processes in the banks to assess the areas of weakness 
with regard to KYC, IPO finance, advances against shares and internal controls 
etc.

the Constitution, 'tax on purchase or sale of goods within a State' is a State subject. Thus, 
the State Sales Tax as well as State VAT (which has been implemented to replace the 
State Sales Tax) is a State subject. An Empowered Committee of State Finance 
Ministers (EC) has been constituted to deliberate upon and decide all matters 
concerning Sales Tax/VAT, including the structure of rates of tax on various 
commodities. Thus, it is for the EC to decide as to which items are to be brought under 
VAT and if so, what would be the rates of tax on such items. 
The EC has decided to keep Motor Spirits (including Petrol, Diesel and Aviation 
Turbine Fuel) outside VAT. These items are subject to 20% floor rate of tax (except 
that the floor rate for Diesel is 12.5% in case of Nprth-Eastern States, Sikkim and 
J&K). States may levy taxes at rates higher than the floor rates for these items. On the 
other hand, the EC has decided to bring certain items under VAT. Out of these items, 
Cooking Gas (LPG), Natural Gas, Naptha, Lubricants, Low Sulphur Heavy Stock 
(LSHS) and Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) are taxable @ 12.5% under VAT and 
PDS kerosene is taxable @ 4%. Since it is a State subject, it is entirely for the EC and 
the State Governments to take a decision in this regard and the Central Government 
has no proposals on this issue.

Cooperation in the field of oil and natural gas between the National 
Development and Reform Commission of the People's Republic of China and the 
Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas of the Republic of India was signed on

Participating Interests in oil and gas projects located in Vietnam, Sudan, Russia, 
Iraq, Iran, Myanmar, Libya, Syria, Australia, Ivory Coast, Qatar and Egypt. 
These companies are aggressively scouting for E&P opportunities in 
countries such as Venezuela, Kazakhstan, Kuwait, Yemen, Chad, Niger, 
Nigeria, Angola, Ecuador etc. in addition to efforts to acquire more assets in the

Promotion of tourism in Himachal Pradesh 
† 280. SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: Will the Minister of TOURISM AND 
CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of States which have attracted maximum number of 
foreign tourists during the last three years; 
(b) the details of schemes implemented by Government especially in 
Himachal Pradesh to attract foreign tourists; 
(c) the profit earned by the tourism sector from the said schemes; and 
(d) the percentage of share of tourism sector in total income earned in term 
of foreign exchange in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF TOURISM AND CULTURE (SHRIMATI 
AMBIKA SONI): (a) As per the estimates, the State of Maharashtra recorded 
maximum foreign tourist visits during 2004 and 2003, while during 
2002,'Tamil Nadu recorded maximum foreign tourist visits. 
(b) There are no State specific sc hemes being implemented by 
Department of Tourism to attract foreign tourists. The Department of Tourism 
however, provides financial assistance to States under its various schemes for 
development of specified destinations/Circuits in States to attract domestic and 
foreign tourists. The Department of Tourism has also launched publicity 
campaign in foreign and domestic markets to show stunning vignettes of India 
through TV, Internet, Magazines, and also by organizing events, facilitation 
participating in tourism parts and bringing out collaterals to attract tourists. The 
State Government is also releasing advertisements in leading magazines and in 
electronic media to attract foreign tour ists, besides participating in tourism 
fairs. 
(c) The foreign exchange earnings by India from tourism during the year 
2005 have been estimated at US$ 5731 million. 
(d)As per the information provided by Reserve Bank of India, share of 
tourism/travel receipts to total fore ign exchange earnings during 2004-05 
was 4.2%.

(d) what is the action plan of Government to complete the projects before 
the end of the Tenth Plan? 
THE MINISTER OF TOURISM AND CULTURE (SHRIMATI 
AMBIKA SONI): (a) Based on proposals received from the State Government 
the Rural Tourism Projects have been sanctioned for following destinations of 
Andhra Pradesh:

(ii) Konaseema, 
(iii) Puttaparthi, 
(iv) Srikalahasti,

identifying the projects. The implementation of the projects sanctioned is the 
responsibility of the State Government concerned. However, the monitoring of 
the implementation of sanctioned projects is done regularly to ensure timely 
completion.

Proposal for linking of small rivers and canals 
296. SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are planning to create smaller links between rivers 
and canals to resolve irregularities of water distribution; and 
(b) if so, the details of the proposals alongwith its status so far? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ): (a) and 
(b) The Ministry of Water Resources (MoWR) and Central Water Commission (CWC) 
formulated a National Perspective Plan (NPP). for Water Resources Development in 1980 
envisaging inter-basin transfer of water from surplus basins to deficit ones. NPP 
comprises of two components, viz. (i) Himalayan rivers development component and 
(ii) Peninsular rivers development component. National Water Development 
Agency (NWDA) was set up in 1982 as a registered Society under MoWR to carry out 
detailed studies for NPP. NWDA, based on water balance and other studies, identified 30 
links (14 under Himalayan and 16 under Peninsular) for preparation of feasibility reports 
(FR). FRs of 16 (2 Himalayan and 14 Peninsular) links have been completed by 
NWDA. Irrigation is a State subject and as per present policy, irrigation projects are 
planned, investigated, formulated, implemented and funded by the State Governments out of 
their own resources and as per their own priorities. Therefore, the works to resolve 
irregularities of water distribution are carried out by State Governments and the 
Central Government does not contemplate smaller links between rivers and canals.

RESOURCE'S be pleased to state:

Pakistani officials recently visited the Baglihar hydroelectric project site for 
inspection; and 
(b) if so, how far the dispute have come nearer to resolution of the issues 
thereby, indicating the precise dispute and how it is sought to be resolved? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (PROF. SAIF-.UD-DIN 
SOZ): (a) Yes, Sir. Prof. Raymond Lafitte, the Neutral Expert appointed to 
examine the matters relating to Baglihar Project had visited the Project 
accompanied by Indian and Pakistani officials on October 2-3, 2005. 
(b) The Government of Pakistan are of the view that certain features of the 
Dam such as the location of power intake, the location of the gated spillways, the 
size of the pondage, the calculated maximum probable flow are not in 
conformity with design parameters as laid down in the Indus Water Treaty, 
1960. The Government of Pakistan filed its Memorial on the case and the 
Government of India has filed its Counter Memorial before the Neutral Expert. 
The respective parties had been given an opportunity to make a site inspection. 
The Expert required India to furnish additional technical reports, which have 
been filed. Thereafter the Government of Pakistan had filed its Reply on the 
points raised and India is to file its Rejoinder as per the time schedule prescribed 
by the Neutral Expert. Thereafter, the two parties will be given an opportunity 
to make oral presentations in the matt er. Thereafter, the Neutral Expert will 
come to his determination on matters referred to him. This determination by 
the Neutral Expert will be made on the basis of his technical assessment of the 
Dam's design proposed by India in relation to the provisions of the Treaty.

(e) Water being a State subject, it is primarily the responsibility of State 
Government concerned for the planning, development, funding, execution 
and management of all type of water resources projects to harness the water

India is promoting the strategies for optimization of water use efficiency, water

Water Resources and Central Water Commission have formulated a National 
Perspective Plan for Water Resources Development in the country which 
envisages inter-linkages between various peninsular rivers and Himalayan

Construction of dams on inter-State rivers 
305. SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN : Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
195 

RAJYA SABHA [21 February, 2006] 
(a) whether State Governments have the authority to construct dam, 
barrier etc. afresh across inter-State rivers unilaterally; 
(b) whether any proposal to construct such dam has been sent to 
the Centre by any State Government; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) in what manner Government would prevent such unlawful 
construction of dams by any State Government? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN 
SOZ): (a) Irrigation is a State subject and as per present policy, irrigation 
projects are planned, investigated, formulated, implemented and funded 
by the State Government out of their own resources and as per their own 
priorities. As per the guidelines of Planning Commission, all major and 
multi-purpose and medium irrigation project and flood control including 
drainage projects which have inter-state ramifications, are techno-
economically appraised in Central Water Commission (CWC) and 
approved by the Advisory Committee on Irrigation Flood Control and Multi-
purpose projects in the Ministry of Water Resources before the investment 
clearance to such projects/schemes is accorded by the Planning 
Commission. As per criteria for techno-economic appraisal followed in 
CWC, projects situated in an inter- state river basin where no tribunal 
decision or valid inter-state agreement is available or where no tribunal 
has been constituted, it is consider ed desirable to get concurrence of 
other co-basin State particularly when substantial adverse impact on other 
co-basin State is anticipated. 
(b) and (c) Upto 15th February, 2006, 190 new major and medium 
irrigation projects from 21 States have been received in CWC for techno-
economic appraisal. 
(d) In such cases, Central Government persuade the concerned 
States through dialogue, discussion and correspondence.

for which we are here debating on the Motion of Thanks consists of 62

not taking note of each of the bullets or each of the points that has been 
made by the President. Nor are we taking into consideration the various 
amendments that have been proposed. This is taken as a debate free for 
all. The opponents would, of course, take the opportunity of attacking the 
ruling Government as if it was an electoral campaign, and the ruling party 
people, particularly those who aspire to get some posts, try to use the 
opportunity for pleasing their bosses. I think this is hardly the correct 
tenor for holding a debate on the Motion of Thanks for the President. I 
would suggest in the proper way later on that this debate on the Motion of 
Thanks should be carried out either on the basis of each of the points 
that is raised by the President or on the basis of amendments that are 
proposed by various members. Othe rwise, the debate would become 
entirely pointless. As far as I see t he debate, the basic situation is like 
this. The deficiencies in infrastructure, whether you are talking of power 
or telephones etc., all came up during the period of socialist planning 
and were inherited by the Government of Shri P.V. Narsimha Rao and 
our present Prime Minister who wa s the then Finance Minister. These 
are the people we have to thank for taking up the challenge and giving 
the entire Indian economy a different turn. (Interruptions) Since then, 
apparently, both the ruling party and the opposition party have lost their 
economic agenda and they are mouthing cliches in order to get advantage 
in elections. Today, the point is not whether we should have socialism or 
we should have economic reforms. That is not the point. The point is 
whether we follow the Arrow's theore m which specifically states that 
community decisions can only be irrational, and against that, the Amartya 
Sen thesis which says that in spite of the Arrow's theorem, there has to 
be some kind of a community action in the fields of hunger, education, 
health, etc. That is really the economic controversy in the present political 
situation. I am afraid, the President, while making the forecast for the 
future has not really grasped the issues and has not really put forward 
the issues that are involved. What has happened is, there are some very 
important issues that have been skirted. For example, FDI in retail trade, 
in my opinion, is a decision that is going to change the entire complexion 
of the Indian economy. As a farmers' movement man, I would say that if

DR. P.C.ALEXANDER (Maharashtra): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I 
would like to avail of this opportunity to raise two or three issues reference 
to which has been conspicuously absent from the speech of the 
Rashtrapati, but which I think deserve the attention of the whole nation if 
we are to maintain the health and vibrance of our democracy. After the 
Rashtrapati's speech last year, a number of developments have taken 
place in this country, some of which give us cause for pride and happiness, 
while some make us feel concerned and unhappy. The most important 
developments, in my opinion, which should have caused us great concern 
as Members of Parliament and which continues to cause great concern 
are the incidents of dishonourable behaviour on the part of some Members 
of Parliament. I am referring to the two incidents of gross corruption alleged 
against some Members of Parliament, one relating to receiving money 
for raising question on the floor of the House, and the other relating to 
the misuse of MPLADS funds. Un fortunately, the weakness of our 
community, of our nation is that we show anger, revulsion, annoyance, 
and outrage when a particular incident of corruption give us a shock, but 
very soon, we forget all about that . And when some new instances of 
gross corruption come to our attention, we forget the earlier one which 
should have been discussed and for which we should have arrived at 
some solution. I have always felt that it is this weakness on the part of 
our nation, which has made us earn the dubious distinction of being one 
of the most corrupt nations in the world I have always felt that if there is 
one factor which prevents us from becoming one of the most advanced 
nations in the world, it is corruption in public life. You may say that many 
other nations also suffer from the sa me disease. But we have all the 
potential to become one of the two or three topmost nations in the world 
if only we handle this problem of corruption in a serious manner. 
Unfortunately, as I said earlier, if something happens we feel outraged, 
and then we forget all about it. We have become tolerant to corruption. 
We have developed a permissive attitude to corruption, and it is this 
tolerance and permissive attitude which is perpetuating this evil in our 
country. Many suggestions have been made as to how this problem should 
be tackled. Many experts have gone into this issue, but I am sorry to say, 
not one set of these suggestions has been accepted or implemented by 
the present or the previous Governments. By mere discussions on the 
floor of the House or bhashans from platforms we can not solve this 
problem. Sometimes, I have a feeling that if only Gandhiji had been given

tackle this problem effectively. His life was spent for laying the

rod for integrity, honesty in public life. Unfortunately, his cruel 
assassination happened immediately after independence, and after 
him, not a single soul has risen in our nation, who could carry the torch

another Gandhiji to arise or another Jai Prakash Narain to arise to lead

tuned, to have that type of a second Messiah who will lead this 
country, this nation, out from the morass into which it has fallen. I 
earnestly -thought, wished that t he President's Address would have 
contained, at least, a small paragraph about the determination of the 
Government to fight corruption and to maintain higher standards of 
probity but the Address disappointed me in that. I will come to the 
second issue. The Government is deciding, in a short while, to give 
help to people to fight elections, help to the political parties to maintain

very great, but, at least, a beginning is likely to be made. But I would 
like to warn the Government and also the Members of Parliament that 
before we decide to use public funds for the maintenance of political 
parties' working or for giving assistance to individuals to fight elections, 
we should insist on all political parties to have within their own 
working, to adopt for their own working, certain standards of 
accountability, certain standards of transparency and also certain 
standards of inner democracy. For 30-40 years the western 
democracies have been trying this practice of helping parties and 
individuals to fight elections and giving public funds. But they have 
also passed necessary legislations to see that the parties maintain 
inner party democracy and remain accountable for the funds that they 
receive and the funds that they  spend. Then only they get the 
entitlement for State aid. But we  are not bothered about it. We are 
thinking of providing State aid to political parties and candidates 
without taking care of the weaknesses of the party system. It does not 
have the inner party

democracy and it does not have accountability to the public. Funds are 
received and funds are spent in crores by some parties. But no audited 
accounts are made available to the public to make the public feel happy 
that these funds are being spent in the right way and for the right reasons. 
The third point that I want to ra ise is about our electoral system. 
The President's in his Address has said that our electoral system has an 
impeccable record and is the pride of the nation. I am afraid, he has not 
used the right word as the subject of the sentence. I would say, the Election 
Commission in India has an impeccable record and is the pride of the 
nation. But I will not subscribe to the view or the statement that the electoral 
system has an impeccable record. Our electoral system, in the past 58 
years of our independence, has not even  assimilated the basic things 
which are necessary for claiming this title of having an impeccable record. 
Its record is very poor. Malpractices have been there in all the elections. 
The role of criminal elements in society has become so conspicuous that 
there is no word to describe what it is. People have been led to march or 
made to march to the polling booths without knowing what they are going 
to vote for or why they are going to vote for a particular candidate. There 
are so many loopholes in our system; there are so many deficiencies in 
our system. Here again, so many committees and commissions have 
recommended what should be done. But very little action has been taken. 
We have this great institution of Election Commission which has to fight 
all the odds that it faces and, in addition to that, face the criticism also. I 
give my tribute whole-heartedly to the manner in which the Election 
Commission has functioned. 
But I would like to tell you, Mr. Deputy Chairman, and I would like to 
inform the Members of the House that we can't continue this system in 
this way for many more elections. There are limits to which an Election 
Commission can go and there are limits to which it can stand the strain. 
One day they will also break down. Look at the frequency of elections. 
Every moment, everyday, every week, every month, there is an election. 
There are elections for the State Assemblies and there are elections for 
the Parliament separately. There are elections for a few groups of States 
and then come elections for another few groups of States. Then comes 
the instability in Government administration at the State level. When the 
code of conduct comes into operation, development schemes are kept 
in abeyance. Then come the movement of police from one State to another

RAJYA SABHA [21 February, 2006] 
State and the movement of civil servants from one place to another place. 
Enormous expenditure is involved. We have to have a system by which 
the country will have elections at a particular time. We have to have a 
system by which if the Government lo ses majority in Parliament, it will 
not go out of office immediately and result in fresh elections, but another 
Government has to be voted in its place by a simultaneous vote of 
affirmative confidence before there is a vacuum created by its resignation. 
Once a Government is elected for five years, it should continue for five 
years, unless in the middle it is thrown out and another Government 
comes in its place. Simultaneously, you can throw out a Government and 
bring in another Government; otherwise, this practice of continuing 
elections from month to month and almost from day to day and everybody 
remaining in an election mode in t he country for days together, is not 
going to be a solution to our problem. The Election Commission may fail 
in its task of commanding the loyalty and approval of the nation on this. 
I will conclude by raising an issue pertaining to the State from which 
I have been elected. It may be a local demand but it is a serious demand 
and that is the demand of the Konkan region of the Maharashtra State to 
have a statutory development board of its own. This would need an 
amendment of article 371 of the Constitution. This amendment had taken 
place and Statutory Development Boards were established for the 
backward regions of Vidarbha and Marathwada, but Konkan was left 
out. The Konkan region is as backw ard as Vidarbha and Marathwada. 
For some reasons, it was left out and it has been tagged along with the 
rest of Maharashtra which includes very advanced places like Pune, 
Mumbai City, Thane and all that. Konkan has not got its legitimate share. 
As one who is responsible for introudcing this new scheme of development 
boards in Maharashtra, I very strongly feel that proper justice has not 
been done to Konkan. The matter is pending with the Government. The 
matter was pending with the previous Government also. No firm decision 
is being taken. I wish to avail of this opportunity to press the importance 
and urgency of this decision. Thank you.

STATEMENTS BY MINISTERS 
Justice Rajindar Sachar Committee 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE): 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, with your permission I make the following statement: 
On 9th March, 2005 a High Level Committee under the chairmanship 
of Justice Rajindar Sachar was set up "for preparation of a report on the 
social economic and educational status of the Muslim community of India." 
According to the 2001 census the Muslims of India formed the largest 
minority group of over 138 million, constituting about 13.4% of the country's 
population. The Muslim community is reportedly afflicted by widespread 
illiteracy, low income and irregular employment implying a higher incidence 
of backwardness relative to other religious groups of India. 
The High Level Committee was mandated to obtain relevant 
information from Departments and Agencies of the Central Government, 
State Governments and also conduct an  intensive literature survey to 
identify published data, articles, research on relative social, economic 
and educational status of the Muslims of India at the State, Regional and 
District levels, to address the reasons for backwardness and to formulate 
appropriate policy to intervene as and when it is necessary. 
The Ministry of Defence in its letter dated 14th September, 2005 
sent to the High Level Committee clea rly brought out that the existing 
policy of the Government on recruitment in the Armed Forces is based 
on merit and is open to every citizen of the country including the members 
of the Muslim community without any discrimination on the basis of their 
caste, creed, religion or region. The Armed Forces are professional, 
apolitical, secular and the most disciplined force the country has today. 
Indian Armed Forces have an all India orientation in which each State 
contributes its fair share of manpower to the Armed Forces.
